svg.aria-label: Illustrative chart: a burst of 48 photo uploads in one minute arrives faster than the Bedrock-limited processing ceiling of 12 images per minute; the SQS queue depth rises to 36 and drains over five minutes, while the side panel compares what each design does with the same burst
svg.text: A burst meets a quota — load levelling
Illustrative numbers. The ceiling is whatever Bedrock allows (requests/min ÷ calls per image), not Lambda or DynamoDB.
48 photos in one minute (an album upload)
only 12 can be processed — 36 are left over
QUEUE DEPTH AT END OF MINUTE · ApproximateNumberOfMessagesVisible
drains at the ceiling rate, 36 → 0 in ~5 min
nothing failed; the work just finished later
The queue does not make Bedrock faster. It turns a rate mismatch from errors into latency —
acceptable here because classification is a side-effect nobody is waiting on.
In CloudWatch this is ApproximateNumberOfMessagesVisible, climbing and then draining.
36 uploads hit ThrottlingException while the user waits.
They see errors and must retry by hand; work not retried
A Bedrock throttle is a function error: Lambda retries it
twice (≈1 min, then ≈2 min) and then hands the event to the
failure destination. Capping reserved concurrency makes
Lambda hold invokes instead (up to 6 h), but that backlog
has no depth you can watch, pause or replay.
The 36 wait in the queue. The worker drains at the ceiling;
throttled messages back off 20 → 40 → 80 → 160 s via
ChangeMessageVisibility. Nothing is lost, and the depth
graph on the left is something you can show and alarm on.
